# 1. Open Stat Prog Modules

From [Open Statistical Programming](https://www.openstatprog.com/) work on the modules:

- Data manipulation

- GGplot visualizations

- Advanced functions

# 2. Hand-in assignment

With this hand-in assignment you demonstrate that you can visualise the relation between two continuous variables with `ggplot()`, and fit and interpret a simple linear regression model with `lm()`.

::: callout-important
## What to hand in

- Hand in **only your rendered `.html` file**. Do not hand in your `.qmd` file or a zip of your project.
- Name your file **`lab2_firstname_lastname_studentnumber.html`**, for example `lab2_jane_doe_1234567.html`.
- Your `.html` file must be **self-contained**: use `embed-resources: true` in your YAML header, so that your plots are stored inside the `.html` file. Without it, your plots will be missing when we open your file.
:::

## The data

In this lab you will use the built-in dataset `iris`, so there is nothing to download. It contains measurements (in centimetres) of 150 iris flowers from three species. You can find more information by typing `?iris` in the console.

**Exercise 2**

Inspect the data with `head()`. Which variables are measured in the first four columns, and in which unit?

```{r, include = params$answers}
head(iris)
```

```{r, include = params$answers, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("**Answer:** The length and width of the sepal leaves (`Sepal.Length`, `Sepal.Width`)",
    "and of the petal leaves (`Petal.Length`, `Petal.Width`), all in centimetres.",
    "The fifth column, `Species`, is the type of flower.\n")
```

## Inspecting the relation between two variables

A good way to eyeball the relation between two continuous variables is a scatterplot. As a reminder, a `ggplot()` is built up in layers that are added with `+`:

- `ggplot(data, aes(x = ..., y = ...))` sets the data and maps variables to the axes;
- a `geom_...()` layer chooses how the data are drawn, for example `geom_point()` for points;
- `labs()` adds axis labels and a title;
- a `theme_...()` layer, such as `theme_minimal()` or `theme_bw()`, changes the overall look.

**Exercise 3**

Make a scatterplot with `Sepal.Length` on the x-axis and `Petal.Width` on the y-axis. Give both axes an informative label (including the unit), add a title and apply a theme.

```{r, include = params$answers}
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Petal.Width)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Sepal length (cm)",
       y = "Petal width (cm)",
       title = "Sepal length and petal width") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Exercise 4**

A smooth curve helps to see the general shape of the relation. You can add one with `geom_smooth()`. With `method = "loess"` you get a flexible curve that follows the data, and `se = FALSE` leaves out the confidence band.

Add a loess curve to your plot from Exercise 3 with `geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE)`.

```{r, include = params$answers, message = FALSE}
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Petal.Width)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Sepal length (cm)",
       y = "Petal width (cm)",
       title = "Sepal length and petal width") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Exercise 5**

Change the loess curve into a straight regression line by using `method = "lm"`. Describe in one sentence the relation that the line shows.

```{r, include = params$answers, message = FALSE}
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Petal.Width)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Sepal length (cm)",
       y = "Petal width (cm)",
       title = "Sepal length and petal width") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r, include = params$answers, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("**Answer:** The line goes up: there is a positive, roughly linear relation.",
    "Flowers with longer sepal leaves tend to have wider petal leaves.\n")
```

## Simple linear regression

With the `lm()` function you specify a linear regression model. The model is always written as `outcome ~ predictor`. You can store the model in an object and ask for the results with `summary()`. The example below predicts petal width from sepal width:

```{r}
iris_model1 <- lm(Petal.Width ~ Sepal.Width, data = iris)

summary(iris_model1)
```

The summary shows:

- the model formula;
- the estimated coefficients, with their standard errors and significance tests;
- information on the residuals;
- an F-test for the model as a whole;
- the (adjusted) R squared, which tells you how much of the variance in the outcome the model explains.

You can also extract parts of the model, for example `coef(iris_model1)` for the coefficients.

**Exercise 6**

Fit a regression model in which `Sepal.Length` is predicted by `Petal.Width`. Store it in an object called `model1` and show its summary. Report the intercept, the regression coefficient and the R squared, each rounded to 2 decimals.

```{r, include = params$answers}
model1 <- lm(Sepal.Length ~ Petal.Width, data = iris)

summary(model1)
```

```{r, include = params$answers, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
model1 <- lm(Sepal.Length ~ Petal.Width, data = iris)
cat("**Answer:** intercept = ", sprintf("%.2f", coef(model1)[1]),
    ", regression coefficient = ", sprintf("%.2f", coef(model1)[2]),
    ", R squared = ", sprintf("%.2f", summary(model1)$r.squared), ".\n", sep = "")
```

**Exercise 7**

Give a substantive interpretation of the regression coefficient of `model1`: what does it say about the flowers?

```{r, include = params$answers, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("**Answer:** For every 1 cm increase in petal width, the predicted sepal length increases by ",
    sprintf("%.2f", coef(model1)[2]), " cm. ",
    "The coefficient is significant (p < .001), and petal width explains about ",
    round(100 * summary(model1)$r.squared), "% of the variance in sepal length.\n", sep = "")
```

**Exercise 8**

Make the plot from Exercise 5 again, but now with `Petal.Width` on the x-axis and `Sepal.Length` on the y-axis, so that it matches `model1`. Does the line in the plot agree with the coefficients from Exercise 6?

```{r, include = params$answers, message = FALSE}
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Petal.Width, y = Sepal.Length)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Petal width (cm)",
       y = "Sepal length (cm)",
       title = "Petal width and sepal length") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r, include = params$answers, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("**Answer:** Yes. `geom_smooth(method = \"lm\")` fits exactly the same regression model, ",
    "so the line has the same intercept (a predicted sepal length of ", sprintf("%.2f", coef(model1)[1]),
    " cm at a petal width of 0) and rises ", sprintf("%.2f", coef(model1)[2]),
    " cm for every cm of petal width.\n", sep = "")
```
